- When sentiment is strongly positive (≥ 0.6) and forecast is rising sharply, reduce peak overshoots by 5–10% to avoid overreacting to sentiment-driven momentum.
- If sentiment is negative (≤ -0.2) and forecast is falling, avoid excessive downward bias — adjust downward only if 3+ consecutive days show negative sentiment and price is trending lower.
- For 30-day forecasts, if the last 5–7 days show strong mean reversion (price oscillating within 2–3% of 14-day moving average), reduce forecast volatility and anchor toward recent mean.
- When sentiment is neutral (0.2–0.4) and price has recently spiked, apply a “cool-down” correction: subtract 2–5% from forecast peak to account for lagged market reaction.
- If forecast consistently overestimates true price by 3–5% in the first 7 days of the 30-day horizon, reduce initial forecast by 1–2% to account for early lag.
- If sentiment is rising but price is flat or declining, reduce forecast slope — sentiment may be overvalued; don’t assume momentum without price confirmation.
- For 30-day forecasts with high volatility in sentiment (±0.3 or more), apply a “sentiment dampening” rule: reduce forecast amplitude by 10–15% to avoid sentiment-driven noise amplification.
